# Overview

`STBench` provides a unified framework for applying and benchmarking
normalisation methods for spatial transcriptomics data.

The package supports a workflow including:

- quality control;
- normalisation;
- spatially variable gene analysis;
- spatial expression visualisation;
- gene-set benchmarking;
- cell-type annotation;
- spatial clustering;
- clustering performance evaluation; and
- gene ontology enrichment analysis.

This vignette demonstrates a typical `STBench` workflow using a
`SpatialExperiment` object.

# Installation

The development version of `STBench` can be installed from GitHub.

```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
# remotes::install_github("USERNAME/STBench")
```

Load the package with:

```{r load-package}
library(STBench)
```

Depending on the analyses performed, additional packages may also be required.

```{r additional-packages, eval=FALSE}
library(SpatialExperiment)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
```

# Input data

`STBench` primarily works with `SpatialExperiment` objects containing a
count matrix and spatial coordinates.

For this vignette, we assume that an object called `spe` has already been
loaded.

```{r inspect-input, eval=FALSE}
spe
```

The object should contain raw counts in the `counts` assay.

```{r inspect-assays, eval=FALSE}
assayNames(spe)
```

For computational efficiency when experimenting with a new workflow, users
may initially work with a subset of genes or spots.

```{r subset-example, eval=FALSE}
spe <- spe[1:500, 1:2000]
```

# Quality control

## Calculate QC metrics

Basic quality-control metrics can be calculated using `add_qc_metrics()`.

```{r qc-metrics, eval=FALSE}
spe_qc <- add_qc_metrics(
  spe = spe,
  assay_name = "counts",
  mito_pattern = "^MT-"
)
```

The resulting object contains additional QC information that can be used for
visualisation and filtering.

## Visualise QC distributions

QC distributions can be inspected with `plot_qc()`.

```{r qc-plots, eval=FALSE}
qc <- plot_qc(
  spe = spe_qc,
  bins = 45,
  show_density = TRUE,
  theme_name = "classic"
)

qc$plot
```

Individual QC panels can also be accessed separately.

```{r individual-qc, eval=FALSE}
qc$plots$library_size
qc$plots$gene_mean
qc$plots$detected_genes
qc$plots$mitochondrial
```

## Explore QC cutoffs

Potential filtering thresholds can be examined before removing observations.

```{r qc-cutoffs, eval=FALSE}
cut <- plot_qc_cutoffs(
  spe = spe_qc,
  library_cutoff = NULL,
  gene_cutoff = NULL,
  n_points = 200,
  theme_name = "classic"
)

cut$plot
```

Candidate thresholds can then be supplied directly.

```{r qc-selected-cutoffs, eval=FALSE}
cut_selected <- plot_qc_cutoffs(
  spe = spe_qc,
  library_cutoff = 2.5,
  gene_cutoff = 0.2,
  n_points = 200,
  theme_name = "classic"
)

cut_selected$plot
```

## Apply QC filtering

Filtering is performed using `filter_qc()`.

```{r qc-filter, eval=FALSE}
spe_filtered <- filter_qc(
  spe = spe_qc,
  library_cutoff = 2.5,
  gene_cutoff = 0.01,
  recalculate = TRUE,
  assay_name = "counts",
  mito_pattern = "^MT-"
)
```

QC distributions can then be reassessed after filtering.

```{r qc-after, eval=FALSE}
qc_after <- plot_qc(
  spe = spe_filtered,
  bins = 45,
  show_density = TRUE,
  theme_name = "classic"
)

qc_after$plot
```

For downstream analyses we use the filtered object.

```{r set-spe-use, eval=FALSE}
spe_use <- spe_filtered
```

# Normalisation

Multiple normalisation methods can be applied through a common interface using
`normalize_spe()`.

```{r normalisation, eval=FALSE}
norm <- normalize_spe(
  spe = spe_use,
  methods = c(
    "none",
    "scran"
  )
)

names(norm)
```

The output is a named list containing the corresponding normalised
`SpatialExperiment` objects.

Additional normalisation methods can be included when their required packages
are installed.

# Spatially variable gene analysis

## Detect spatially variable genes

Spatially variable genes can be identified using `run_svg()`.

```{r svg-analysis, eval=FALSE}
svg <- run_svg(
  norm_list = norm,
  method = "nnSVG",
  verbose = TRUE
)

names(svg)
```

For illustration, select a small collection of genes.

```{r select-genes, eval=FALSE}
genes_use <- rownames(spe_use)[1:5]
```

## Compare SVG statistics

SVG statistics can be compared across normalisation methods.

```{r svg-stat, eval=FALSE}
svg_stat <- plot_svg_stat(
  svg_norm = svg,
  genes = genes_use,
  stat = "LR_stat",
  transform = "log"
)

svg_stat$plot
```

## Compare SVG ranks

The corresponding SVG ranks can also be visualised.

```{r svg-rank, eval=FALSE}
svg_rank <- plot_svg_rank(
  svg,
  genes = genes_use
)

svg_rank$plot
```

# Spatial expression visualisation

Spatial expression patterns can be compared across normalisation methods using
`plot_spatial_expression()`.

## Scaled expression

Expression values can be scaled to facilitate comparison of spatial patterns.

```{r spatial-expression-scaled, eval=FALSE}
p_scaled <- plot_spatial_expression(
  norm_list = norm,
  genes = genes_use,
  assay_name = "logcounts",
  scale_expr = TRUE,
  point_size = 0.5,
  colour_option = "magma",
  theme_name = "classic"
)

p_scaled$plot
```

## Unscaled expression

Original normalised expression values can also be displayed.

```{r spatial-expression-original, eval=FALSE}
p_original <- plot_spatial_expression(
  norm_list = norm,
  genes = genes_use,
  assay_name = "logcounts",
  scale_expr = FALSE,
  point_size = 0.5,
  colour_option = "magma",
  ncol_genes = 1,
  theme_name = "classic"
)

p_original$plot
```

# Gene-set benchmarking

Known gene sets can be used to evaluate how different normalisation methods
affect SVG detection.

## Distribution of SVG statistics

For example, a set of housekeeping or stable genes can be examined.

```{r gene-set-distribution, eval=FALSE}
stable <- plot_svg_gene_set_distribution(
  svg,
  genes = Housekeeping_Genes$Gene.name,
  stat = "LR_stat",
  transform = "log",
  plot_type = "boxplot"
)

stable$plot
```

## Gene-set representation among top SVGs

The proportion of genes from a selected gene set among the highest-ranked SVGs
can also be calculated.

```{r gene-set-topn, eval=FALSE}
topn <- plot_svg_topn_gene_set(
  svg_list = svg,
  genes = Housekeeping_Genes$Gene.name,
  top_n = c(
    10,
    20,
    50,
    100
  )
)

topn$plot
```

# Cell-type annotation

Cell-type annotation can be performed for each normalisation method using
`run_annotation()`.

A suitable reference dataset and corresponding cell-type labels must first be
provided.

```{r annotation, eval=FALSE}
annotation_results <- run_annotation(
  norm_list = norm,
  ref = ref,
  labels = ref$cell_type_spec,
  de.method = "wilcox"
)
```

## Spatial annotation maps

```{r annotation-spatial, eval=FALSE}
p_annotation <- plot_spatial_annotation(
  annotation_list = annotation_results,
  label_col = "SingleR_label",
  ncol = 2
)

p_annotation$plot
```

## Cell-type proportions

```{r annotation-proportions, eval=FALSE}
p_celltype <- plot_celltype_proportion(
  annotation_list = annotation_results,
  label_col = "SingleR_label"
)

p_celltype$plot
```

## Annotation agreement

Agreement in cell-type assignments across normalisation methods can be
assessed using:

```{r annotation-agreement, eval=FALSE}
p_agree <- plot_annotation_agreement(
  norm_list = annotation_results,
  annotation_col = "SingleR_label"
)

p_agree$plot
```

# Spatial clustering

`STBench` provides an interface for running BANKSY independently for each
normalisation method.

```{r banksy, eval=FALSE}
banksy_norm <- run_banksy_individual(
  norm_list = norm,
  cluster_col = "banksy_cluster",
  k_geom = 15,
  lambda = 0.8,
  resolution = 0.2,
  seed = 123
)
```

Cluster assignments can be inspected directly.

```{r banksy-table, eval=FALSE}
table(banksy_norm$none$banksy_cluster)
table(banksy_norm$scran$banksy_cluster)
```

## Spatial clustering maps

```{r banksy-spatial, eval=FALSE}
cluster_plot <- plot_spatial_clustering(
  norm_list = banksy_norm,
  cluster_col = "banksy_cluster",
  method_order = c(
    "none",
    "scran"
  ),
  point_size = 0.5
)

cluster_plot$plot
```

# Clustering performance

When ground-truth biological labels are available, clustering performance can
be quantified using the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI).

## Calculate ARI

```{r ari-calculate, eval=FALSE}
ari_results <- calculate_ari(
  norm_list = banksy_norm,
  ground_truth_col = "layer_guess",
  cluster_col = "banksy_cluster"
)

ari_results
```

## Visualise ARI

```{r ari-plot, eval=FALSE}
ari_plot <- plot_ari(
  ari_df = ari_results,
  method_order = c(
    "none",
    "scran"
  )
)

ari_plot$plot
```

Higher ARI values indicate greater agreement between the inferred spatial
clusters and the supplied reference labels.

# Gene ontology enrichment

Cluster-specific marker genes can be identified and used for downstream Gene
Ontology enrichment analysis.

The appropriate organism annotation package must be supplied through `OrgDb`.

```{r go-analysis, eval=FALSE}
go_results <- calculate_go(
  norm_list = banksy_norm,
  cluster_col = "banksy_cluster",
  methods = c(
    "none",
    "scran"
  ),
  OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db::org.Hs.eg.db
)
```

## Marker genes

The top marker genes used for enrichment analysis can be visualised with:

```{r go-genes, eval=FALSE}
go_genes_plot <- plot_go_genes(
  go_results = go_results,
  top_n = 5,
  method_order = c(
    "none",
    "scran"
  )
)

go_genes_plot$plot
```

## GO enrichment results

```{r go-plot, eval=FALSE}
go_plot <- plot_go(
  go_results = go_results,
  top_n = 5,
  method_order = c(
    "none",
    "scran"
  )
)

go_plot$plot
```

# Summary

`STBench` provides a consistent workflow for comparing normalisation methods
across several downstream spatial transcriptomics analyses.

A typical analysis consists of:

1. performing quality control;
2. applying one or more normalisation methods;
3. detecting spatially variable genes;
4. examining spatial expression patterns;
5. benchmarking predefined gene sets;
6. evaluating cell-type annotations;
7. performing spatial clustering;
8. comparing clustering accuracy; and
9. assessing cluster-specific biological enrichment.

The same framework allows results from different normalisation approaches to
be generated and compared using a common interface.
